To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the absence of the ER response is a hereditary, recessive trait, (2) high levels of ER are associated with the occurrence of hereditary cancer, and (3) the ER response can be used as a marker to identify carriers of hereditary cancer syndromes at a very early age.

the absence of enhanced reactivation of UV-C-irradiaed HSV-1 in XP cells is heritable, and that the enhanced reactivation response in Li-Fraumenis syndrome and in a family predisposed for breast, colon, ovarian, and stomach cancer is heritable and positively correlated with the occurrence of tumors.

the absence of the enhanced reactivation response (ER) is a heritable trait that is not related to the DNA repair deficiency in xerodermapigmentosum (XP); that the ER response is abnormally induced in cells from Li-Fraumenicancer-prone (LFS) families, and that the ER response may be a prognostic tool for identifying carriers at a young age; and that the ER is abnormally induced also in cells from families with a high incidenceof
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a novel, simple and non-invasive method for the early detection of carriers in hereditary cancer-proneness, based on abnormal expression of the SOS-like stress response in skin fibroblastic cells.

the identification of genes involved in the regulation of the ER response, the elucidation of their role in the pathogenesis of cancer, and the development of a prognostic assay for the identification of carriers at an early age.

the identification of genetic markers that can be used for the early detection of cancer-prone syndomes, as well as for the identification of carriers in families with a high incidence for breast, ovarian, stomach, and colorectal cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

(1) XP patients have an inherited defect in DNA repair; (2) XP cells are deficient in ER; (3) LFS cells are deficient in DNA repair; and (4) LFS and cancer-prone cells are deficient in the ER response.
the ER response, in contrast to EM, is not a general marker of DNA repair deficiency, since the ER response was absent in two XP patients, whereas EM was induced.
XP is characterized by the lack of ER, whereas in LFS, the high incidence of ER is positively correlated with cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have found that the ER response is a hereditary marker for predisposition to cancer in a number of cancer-prone syndrromes.

the ER phenotype is inherited in a non-Mendelian fashion in a family with XP, in a family with LFS, and in a family that is cancer-prone, and that the ER phenotype can possibly be used for genetic counseling in these families.

in xerodermapigmentosum, the absence of ER in UV-exposed skin fiboblasts is a hereditary phenotype, not correlated with repair deficiency, and that in LFS, the presence of abnormally high levels in ER in UV-irradiated cells is a hereditary, predisposing trait.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ER can be used as a biomarker for the presence of a predisposing gene in hereditary cancer-proneness.
the ER phenotype is a heritable trait that can be used to identify carriers in cancer-prone families.
the ER response is a good prognostic marker for cancer-prone syndomes.
